subject: Climate & Environment
title: WHO Air Quality Guidelines
description: A quick, practical guide to WHO Air Quality Guidelines.

hook.text: In 2021, the WHO tightened its air quality guidelines for the first time in 16 years.

buildup.text: The new PM2.5 limit dropped from 10 to 5 micrograms per cubic meter — half the old standard.

discovery.text: Almost no country on Earth currently meets the new guideline. Most are far above it.

twist.text: The guidelines aren't legally binding. Countries can ignore them without consequence.

climax.text: But they set the scientific benchmark — the number governments are judged against.

punchline.text: Science set the bar. The world hasn't reached it yet.

quiz.question: What is the WHO's 2021 PM2.5 guideline?

details.summary: The World Health Organization publishes air quality guidelines recommending safe concentration limits for key pollutants. The 2021 update tightened PM2.5 guidance to 5 micrograms per cubic meter annually, a level almost no country currently meets.
details.whyItMatters: WHO guidelines serve as the global benchmark against which national standards are judged. The tightened 2021 targets highlight how far most countries still need to go.
takeaways: The 2021 annual PM2.5 guideline is 5 micrograms per cubic meter
Almost no country currently meets the updated PM2.5 standard
Guidelines cover PM, ozone, NO2, SO2, and carbon monoxide

faq.question: Are WHO air quality guidelines legally binding?
faq.answer: No, they are recommendations based on the best available health evidence. Countries set their own legally binding national standards, which are often less strict than WHO guidelines due to economic and political considerations.

faq.question: Why did the WHO tighten PM2.5 limits in 2021?
faq.answer: New epidemiological studies showed health damage at concentrations previously considered safe. The annual PM2.5 guideline was halved from 10 to 5 micrograms per cubic meter to reflect this stronger evidence.
